title: Episode 175: Harry S. Truman: The Manhattan Project, Potsdam, and Hiroshima (1945)
description:
On the evening of April 12, 1945, Vice President Harry S. Truman was summoned urgently to the White House. Meeting Eleanor Roosevelt in her second-floor study, he heard the quiet words: 'Harry, the President is dead.' When Truman asked if there was anything he could do for her, Eleanor replied: 'Is there anything we can do for you? For you are the one in trouble now.' Truman had been vice president for only eighty-two days, having met privately with Roosevelt just twice. Shockingly, Truman had never been told about the top-secret two-billion-dollar Manhattan Project. Thrust into supreme command of a global war, Truman confronted the Potsdam Conference, stared down Joseph Stalin, and made the most agonizing and consequential decision in military history: unleashing the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki to end World War II. Discover the trial by fire of America's thirty-third president.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into one of the most dramatic moments of the modern presidency. In April 1945, a modest Midwesterner who had never attended college was suddenly handed the reigns of the world's most powerful nation—and the secret of the ultimate weapon of destruction. Here is George with the story of Harry S. Truman, the revelation of the Manhattan Project, and the dawn of the atomic age.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'THE MOON, THE STARS, AND ALL THE PLANETS'
On Thursday afternoon, April 12, 1945, Vice President Harry S. Truman presided over a sleepy debate in the United States Senate. After adjourning the session, he walked to the Capitol office of House Speaker Sam Rayburn for a late-afternoon bourbon and political gossip—a ritual affectionately known as the 'Board of Education.' Just as he poured a glass, Rayburn handed him a telephone receiver; White House press secretary Steve Early urged him to come to the executive mansion immediately and quietly by the front entrance. Arriving at the White House at five-twenty-five, Truman was ushered upstairs to Eleanor Roosevelt's private study. Eleanor placed a gentle hand upon his shoulder: 'Harry, the President is dead.' A stunned Truman stammered: 'Is there anything I can do for you?' Eleanor looked into his eyes and replied with haunting clarity: 'Is there anything we can do for you? For you are the one in trouble now.' At seven-o-nine that evening, Truman took the oath of office in the Cabinet Room, his hand trembling on a small Gideon Bible. The following morning, surrounded by reporters in the Capitol corridor, Truman uttered words that captured his profound humility: 'Boys, if you ever pray, pray for me now. I don't know if you fellows ever had a load of hay fall on you, but when they told me yesterday what had happened, I felt like the moon, the stars, and all the planets had fallen on me.' In that quiet study on Pennsylvania Avenue, a humble Midwesterner who had never aspired to supreme power found himself entrusted with the destiny of the entire free world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE HABERDASHER OF INDEPENDENCE
Harry S. Truman was unlike any president who had preceded him in the twentieth century. Born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884, he was the last American president who did not possess a college degree. He grew up on a farm near Independence, read voraciously in world history, and became an accomplished classical pianist. During World War I, despite poor eyesight that required thick spectacles, thirty-three-year-old Truman volunteered for combat duty in France, commanding Battery D of the 129th Field Artillery. In the hellish mud of the Meuse-Argonne offensive, Captain Truman won the lifelong devotion of his unruly Irish Catholic troops by standing firm under German artillery barrages. Returning home, he married his childhood sweetheart, Bess Wallace, and opened a men's clothing haberdashery in downtown Kansas City. When the post-war recession forced the store into bankruptcy in 1922, Truman refused to declare personal bankruptcy, laboring for fifteen agonizing years to repay every single creditor in full. Entering local politics under the sponsorship of Kansas City Democratic boss Tom Pendergast, Truman served as an honest, incorruptible county judge, building modern highways and courthouses. Elected to the Senate in 1934, he won national acclaim during World War II as chairman of the 'Truman Committee,' fearlessly investigating defense waste and corporate profiteering, saving fifteen billion dollars and thousands of American lives without a single dissenting report. Truman's reputation for unyielding personal honesty and fiscal integrity during his Senate investigations made him the one man in Washington whom both parties trusted implicitly.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE REVELATION OF THE ATOMIC SECRET
Following his swearing-in on the evening of April 12, Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson pulled the new president aside. Stimson whispered that the military was developing a new explosive of 'almost unbelievable destructive power,' but offered no further details. It was not until twelve days later, on April 25, that Stimson and General Leslie R. Groves, military director of the Manhattan Project, arrived secretly at the White House with a comprehensive memorandum. Truman was stunned to learn that for three years, hidden beneath the codename 'Manhattan District,' the United States had spent two billion dollars—operating secret cities at Oak Ridge, Tennessee; Hanford, Washington; and Los Alamos, New Mexico—to build the world's first atomic bomb based on nuclear fission. One hundred and thirty thousand scientists, engineers, and workers were racing against the terrifying possibility that Nazi Germany might build the weapon first. As Stimson bluntly informed Truman: 'Within four months, we shall in all probability have completed the most terrible weapon ever known in human history, one bomb of which could destroy a whole city.' Truman realized that the ultimate moral burden of human history had landed squarely upon his shoulders. The sheer magnitude of the secret Manhattan Project revealed the astonishing industrial and scientific capacity of a mobilized democracy operating under total wartime discipline.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE POTSDAM CONFERENCE AND THE TRINITY TEST
In July 1945, Truman traveled across the Atlantic aboard the cruiser USS Augusta to Potsdam, outside the ruined ashes of Berlin, for his first and only face-to-face summit with Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin. On the evening of July 16, as negotiations were underway in Cecilienhof Palace, an urgent coded cable arrived from Washington: 'Babies satisfactorily born.' At five-twenty-nine that morning in the desert of Alamogordo, New Mexico, the 'Trinity' test had detonated the world's first plutonium bomb, unleashing an incandescent blast equal to twenty-one thousand tons of TNT that lit up the desert mountains and vaporized a one-hundred-foot steel tower. Armed with this terrifying knowledge, Truman found his confidence transformed. On July 24, Truman casually approached Stalin during a recess, mentioning that the United States possessed a new weapon of unusual destructive force. Stalin smiled blandly, replied that he hoped the Americans would make good use of it against the Japanese, and walked away. Unknown to Truman, Soviet atomic spy Klaus Fuchs had already provided detailed technical blueprints of the bomb to Moscow; Stalin immediately cabled his scientists to redouble their efforts. The blinding detonation at Alamogordo signaled the arrival of an ominous new era where humanity possessed the apocalyptic capacity to annihilate its own civilization in an instant.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE AGONIZING CALCULATION OF OPERATION DOWNFALL
While Nazi Germany had surrendered on May 8, 1945, the Empire of Japan showed no willingness to surrender unconditionally. The brutal battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa had revealed the terrifying fanaticism of Japanese resistance: on Okinawa alone, over twelve thousand Americans were killed, while more than one hundred and ten thousand Japanese soldiers and seventy thousand civilians died, many leaping off cliffs rather than surrender. American intelligence intercepted Japanese operational plans for 'Ketsu-Go'—the defense of the home islands—mobilizing millions of soldiers, ten thousand kamikaze aircraft, and a civilian militia armed with bamboo spears under the slogan: 'One Hundred Million Die Together for the Emperor.' Joint Chiefs of Staff estimates for 'Operation Downfall,' the planned two-stage amphibious invasion of Kyushu and Honshu set for November 1945 and March 1946, projected hundreds of thousands of Allied casualties and millions of Japanese deaths. When the Potsdam Declaration of July 26 demanded Japan's immediate unconditional surrender or face 'prompt and utter destruction,' Tokyo's prime minister publicly announced that the government would 'mokusatsu' the ultimatum—killing it with contemptuous silence. Truman hesitated no longer. Faced with intelligence reports of millions of Japanese civilians prepared to sacrifice their lives in defense of the mainland, Truman sought the fastest possible termination of the slaughter.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: HIROSHIMA, NAGASAKI, AND THE EMPEROR'S SURRENDER
At eight-fifteen on the morning of August 6, 1945, a lone American B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, flew over the Japanese industrial city of Hiroshima. From thirty-one thousand feet, the bombardier released 'Little Boy,' a nine-thousand-pound uranium bomb. Forty-three seconds later, at nineteen hundred feet above the Shima Surgical Clinic, the weapon detonated in a blinding purple flash. A fireball hotter than the surface of the sun vaporized seventy thousand human beings in a fraction of a second, collapsing five square miles of the city into incandescent ash, followed by a towering mushroom cloud of black smoke and radioactive rain. Still, the Japanese military council refused to surrender. Three days later, on August 9, a second bomb, the plutonium weapon 'Fat Man,' was dropped on Nagasaki, killing another forty thousand people, while the Soviet Red Army invaded Japanese-occupied Manchuria with one million troops. Convinced that continued defiance meant the total annihilation of the Japanese race, Emperor Hirohito intervened in an unprecedented imperial conference, deciding to 'bear the unbearable.' On August 15, Hirohito's recorded voice was broadcast over Japanese radio for the first time in history, announcing Japan's surrender. World War II was over. The horrific devastation of Hiroshima and Nagasaki forced the Japanese military oligarchy to accept the reality of unconditional defeat, finally ending the global nightmare of World War II.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: 'THE BUCK STOPS HERE' AND THE VERDICT OF HISTORY
Harry Truman never flinched from the decision to use the atomic bomb. He maintained on his desk in the Oval Office a famous wooden sign reading: 'The Buck Stops Here.' He argued steadfastly throughout his life that the bomb had ended the war in days, saved hundreds of thousands of young American soldiers who would have died storming Japanese beaches, and spared millions of Japanese citizens from prolonged starvation, conventional firebombing, and imperial suicide. Yet Truman was acutely aware that a terrible new threshold had been crossed in human history. As he cautioned in his radio broadcast to the nation following Hiroshima: 'We must constitute ourselves trustees of this new force, to prevent its misuse, and to turn it into the channels of service to all mankind.' A modest farm boy from Missouri had stepped into the shoes of a giant, made the most cataclysmic decision in the annals of warfare, and ushered humanity into the perilous dawn of the nuclear era. Truman's enduring willingness to take personal moral responsibility for the atomic bomb remains a masterclass in presidential accountability in the face of unimaginable tragedy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Harry S. Truman ended World War II and confronted the dawn of the atomic age with the unvarnished courage of a frontier Missourian. Yet peace brought no tranquility: the collapse of the wartime alliance with the Soviet Union sparked the Cold War, labor strikes paralyzed American industry, and Truman's political fortunes sank so low that every newspaper predicted his utter annihilation in the election of 1948. Next week, we turn to the second half of the Truman saga: the whistle-stop train miracle, the Chicago Tribune headline 'Dewey Defeats Truman,' the Marshall Plan, and the brutal crucible of the Korean War. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
